result:
I woke up today with the blinds half open and the light coming in like it has for a million mornings before, thin and honest. The cat was already on the radiator. She does that when the heating has been on too long. I made coffee and watched the steam write little ghosts on the kitchen window. There is a certain kind of freedom in not having a plan for the day. The inbox can wait. The laundry can wait. For about twenty minutes, I can just exist in the small rectangle of my apartment with the kettle ticking and the traffic three floors down.

I think a lot about how we used to be told to make the most of every minute. Use a planner. Optimize. Now I am suspicious of that advice. Some minutes are meant to be wasted. Some minutes are meant to be foggy and warm and unproductive. The best thoughts I have ever had came while I was doing nothing in particular. Waiting for a bus. Brushing my teeth. Staring at the ceiling after a bad dream.

When I was a kid, I believed that writing was a way to keep things from disappearing. I kept notebooks in the backs of books, in shoeboxes, in the glove compartment of my parents' car. I wrote about the dog who died, about the first time I got kissed behind the bleachers, about the way my grandmother's kitchen smelled like cinnamon and old wood. I thought if I wrote it down, it would be safe. It is funny how much is still gone. The notebooks got lost in moves. The memories faded at the edges. The sentences I was so proud of now read like someone else wrote them. That is probably okay.

I read somewhere that memory is not a recording. It is a story we keep retelling to ourselves until it feels true. Every time we recall something, we rewrite it a little. We smooth the rough parts. We add dialogue that probably never happened. I do that with my father’s laugh. It has gotten louder in my head over the years. Maybe because I miss it.

There is a park two blocks from my building that I walk through even when I have nowhere to be. The benches are the same benches. The old man with the red hat feeds pigeons every Tuesday. A woman runs with headphones on at exactly 7:15. The trees are different each year, of course. They get bigger, they lose branches, they get replaced. The park stays the same and does not stay the same, which is the most honest thing about it.

I have been thinking about conversation lately, the kind that happens between people who have nothing to prove. Not networking. Not performing. Just talking. It is rare. Most of the time we are rehearsing our next line while the other person is speaking. We are thinking about how we sound. We are editing. I try to practice listening like it is a skill, like playing an instrument. You have to put the instrument down to hear the room.

If you ask me what I want, I don’t have a tidy answer. I want more quiet. I want to be able to sit in a café and not reach for my phone. I want to remember names. I want to be kinder to myself on the days when I am slow. I want to write things that matter to me even if no one reads them. I want to be able to say I love you and mean it and not feel the need to explain it.

There is a line of a poem I love that goes something like “the world is full of magic things, patiently waiting for our senses to grow sharper.” I think that is true. We get used to the extraordinary because it is always there. The first rain after a dry spell. The way a stranger smiles when you hold the door. The sudden, absurd beauty of a city at 3 a.m. We train ourselves to look past it.

I wonder what people will remember about this time. Not the headlines. The headlines change. I think they will remember the small rituals. The way they made tea. The way they called their mother on Sundays. The way they laughed at a meme that only made sense for six months. The way they tried, imperfectly, to be decent.

I am not sure what I am supposed to be doing with this life I have been given. It feels too big for any single plan. Some days I feel like I am building something, other days I feel like I am just keeping the lights on. Both are work. Both are love.

The cat is off the radiator now. She is looking at me with that expression that means she wants to be fed or she wants me to move so she can sit where I am sitting. I will move. I will make more coffee. I will open the window a little because the air outside smells like rain coming. I will write for a while longer, not because I have something important to say, but because saying things out loud, even to a blank page, keeps me company.

If you are reading this, thank you for being here. It is strange and wonderful that we can sit together in our separate rooms and share a moment. I hope you have a good day. I hope you notice something small and beautiful and let it stay with you. I hope you are gentle with yourself. I hope you find at least twenty minutes where you don’t have to be anything at all.
